## Question

Robertson's reaction starts with pure A. The three concentrations are
needed at t = 40{claim:t_final}, each with a relative error below
1e-4{claim:target}; the reference values are A = 0.715827{claim:y1_ref},
B = 9.185535e-6{claim:y2_ref} and C = 0.284163746{claim:y3_ref}. Which of
the explicit Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) and the Rosenbrock ROS2 delivers that
for the least work, counted as right-hand-side evaluations plus three per
Jacobian? The budget applies to B too, five orders of magnitude smaller
than A, and costs matter to a factor of about 2, the spacing of the
tolerances tried.

## Scales and estimate

A and C change on a time scale of tens; B is created and destroyed on a
scale of 1 / (k3 y3 + 2 k2 y2), a few times 1e-4. The Jacobian's most
negative eigenvalue at t = 40 is -3392.8{claim:lambda_40}. An explicit
step is stable only while h |lambda| stays below about 2.5, so with
|lambda| around 3000 over most of the interval BS3(2) needs about
40 * 3000 / 2.5 steps. My estimate, before any run, was 5e4{estimate:bs_steps}.
ROS2 is L-stable, so its step is limited only by accuracy.

## Model and assumptions

Mass-action kinetics with constant rates; y1 + y2 + y3 = 1 is conserved.
The reference is BS3(2) at a tolerance of 1e-10; ROS2 at the same
tolerance differs from it by at most 6.8e-11{claim:ref_diff}, and both
agree with the published value to about 1e-10, so the reference's error
is negligible against the budget. Tolerances are tried from 1e-1 down in
steps of sqrt(10), with atol = rtol * 1e-6, far below B's scale. The cost
leaves out ROS2's two 3x3 linear solves per step, about the work of one
right-hand side each for three species; that factor is small against the
ratio found.

## Method choice

BS3(2) first meets the budget at rtol 3.16e-5{claim:bs_rtol}, with an
error of 3.39e-5{claim:bs_err} in 45523{claim:bs_steps} steps. ROS2 meets
it at rtol 1e-4{claim:ro_rtol}, with an error of 7.68e-5{claim:ro_err}
in 691{claim:ro_steps} steps.

That costs 182116{claim:bs_cost} for BS3(2) against 3465{claim:ro_cost}
for ROS2: the explicit method is 52.6{claim:cost_ratio} times as
expensive. I choose ros2{claim:choice}.

The explicit method's cost is not about accuracy: with the tolerance at
1e-2 it still takes 45496{claim:bs_steps_loose} steps, against
45523{claim:bs_steps} at its budget tolerance. Its step is pinned by
stability to B's fast mode long after B itself has stopped changing.

## Verification

With fixed steps on the rotation y1' = y2, y2' = -y1, the observed orders
are 2.989{claim:bs_order} for BS3(2) and 2.031{claim:ro_order} for ROS2,
for steps from 0.00625{claim:order_h_min} to 0.05{claim:order_h_max};
the theory says 3 and 2.

From t = 20 to 40 the controller's mean explicit step times |lambda| is
2.520{claim:stab_hlam}, and BS3's stability function reaches -1 at
2.512745{claim:stab_boundary}: the adaptive controller found the
stability limit on its own, as a step size that keeps being accepted
just below it.

Both chosen runs keep y1 + y2 + y3 = 1 to 8.44e-15{claim:mass_err}, as
methods of this kind must for a linear invariant.

## Validation

Verification says the integrators are right; it does not say the answer
is physical. With the common setting atol = rtol = 1e-4, which is above B's
whole value, BS3(2) accepted every step it took until its step size
underflowed at t = 0.0419{claim:naive_bs_t}, and the smallest
concentration it accepted was -3.6e6{claim:naive_bs_ymin}: a blow-up the
controller could not see, because B's error, and the unstable mode that
lives in B, were all below atol. ROS2 with the same setting stays bounded
but misses the budget with an error of 5.4e-4{claim:naive_ro_err}. The
absolute tolerance has to be set by the smallest component that matters.

## Uncertainty and sensitivity

The chosen runs meet the budget with margins of about 3 (BS3) and 1.3
(ROS2); the next looser tolerance fails for both, so the costs are within a
factor of about 2 of the true minimum.

With the two fast reactions 1000{claim:robust_factor} times slower, the
most negative eigenvalue at t = 40 is only -36.8{claim:robust_lambda}.
BS3(2) then costs 3248{claim:robust_bs_cost} and ROS2
7690{claim:robust_ro_cost}: the cheaper method is bs{claim:robust_choice},
so the conclusion fails{claim:robust_holds}. The choice belongs to the
stiffness, not to the chemistry's look.

## Claims and limits

For Robertson's rates, ROS2 meets a 1e-4 budget for about fifty times less
work than BS3(2), because the explicit method's step is held at its
stability limit by a mode whose own contribution is negligible. For rates a
thousand times slower the explicit method is the cheaper. The conclusion was
tested up to t = 40{claim:valid_t_max} at a budget of
1e-4{claim:valid_target}, for three species, counting Jacobians as three
right-hand sides and ignoring linear solves. It says nothing about longer
times, larger systems, where solves dominate, or other methods.
